claims.text: The initial Mg-Al-Cr-Fe powder system exhibits elemental segregation.
The initial Mg-Al-Cr-Fe system contains a mixture of FCC and BCC phases.
Sluggish diffusion at standard sintering temperatures causes the initial phase mixture and segregation.
Adding 2–5 wt% Mn or Cu lowers the activation energy for solid-state diffusion in Mg-Al-Cr-Fe at 850–900 °C.
Accelerated diffusion at 850–900 °C enables formation of a single-phase BCC solid solution before significant Mg volatility or Cr-rich segregation occurs.
The 800–1000 °C processing window represents a balance between densification and Mg volatility.
Pressure-assisted SPS enhances densification kinetics in the proposed alloy.
Mn or Cu creates transient high-concentration diffusion paths in the Mg-Al-Cr-Fe matrix.
Mn or Cu locally distorts the lattice and thereby lowers barriers for Mg and Cr migration.
Mn or Cu acts as a diffusion catalyst through lattice strain.
Comparable lattice-distortion-driven diffusion acceleration has been observed in high-entropy phosphides or alloys.
Al favors BCC-phase formation in a multi-component transition-metal alloy.
Negative Al mixing enthalpy and high configurational entropy drive formation of the proposed BCC phase.
The optimized treatment will produce greater than 95% theoretical density.
The optimized treatment will produce a single-phase BCC microstructure with uniform elemental distribution.
Eliminating Cr-rich and Cr-poor regions improves corrosion resistance by removing galvanic micro-couples.
Samples sintered at 1000 °C suffer Mg volatility, whereas samples sintered at 800 °C suffer incomplete densification and segregation.
Standard additive-free sintering produces less than 90% relative density and poor corrosion resistance in Mg-Al-Cr-Fe.
Above 950 °C, Mg vapor pressure exceeds 10^-3 Pa and causes porosity and density loss.
An Mn or Cu concentration above 10 wt% may induce brittle intermetallic formation.
